Consider Achilles and the hare.

The hare takes off, at speed R.

After a time, T, it will have traveled a distance D, of RT, since we know that distance traveled is equal to the rate of travel multiplied by the time of travel.

Now, at time T, Achilles takes off at speed S which is 2R. After another period of time T, bringing the total for the race to 2T, both Achilles and the hare will have traveled 2D since their distances are now ST and R2T, respectively.

After a third period of time T Achilles will have traveled 2R2T (S2T), while the rabbit will only have traveled R3T. Simplifying, we see that Achilles's D is equal to 4RT while the hare's is only 3RT.

Now, obviously, depending on what you fill in for the R, it will take Achilles more or less time to overtake the hare, but it is plainly obvious that any body traveling faster than another will overtake the other if given enough time.

Yeah, the Fermi Paradox makes so many assumptions that it's practically worthless beyond pop science speculation.

First is the problem of commonality. The obvious assumption is that other civilizations will use electromagnetic manipulation tech (radio and such) as the basis for communications and the like, just like we did. However, who's to say they didn't develop along a different technological path, or one incompatible with our own? Even humans today are using communication technologies that would stump the Fermi Paradox of 40 years ago - due to the shift to digital communications through ground lines and directional radio, Earth's overall radio footprint into space is miniscule compared to that of the mid 20th century, and will only go down as advances in optical communications improve (fiber optics and lasers). On top of that, even our radio signature attenuates as it spread out into space, to the point where our signals are indistinguishable from noise a few light years out. And we only broadcasted in radio for 50 years! Any other civilization, to detect us, would have to be EXACTLY (distance - 50) light years behind us, on the EXACT same technological path, and the signal would have to defy physics to be legible!

On top of that, we assume that - even if we detected life - we would recognize life if we saw it. Pulsar stars, for instance, have a regular "pulse" rhythm for radiation bursts. This is a natural process, for all we know, but what's to say that Pulsars aren't actually the product of some civilization using them as communications? Or that the random static radiation bursts we detect every once in awhile - assumed to be products of vast cosmic explosions - aren't the long-dead messages of other civilizations? Or that the random tachyons we happen to detect on occasion aren't bits in a base-17 digital message across the cosmos? All hypothetical situations, to be sure, but the point is we would never know.

And then you run into the problem of the universe being a lot bigger than the human mind can really imagine, as you showed in your figures - even if life was common, it'd have to be literally popping out of the seams for two civilizations to emerge close enough together in space and time to interact meaningfully.

The "Great Filter" is time and space itself, not anything so dramatic as rarity or the evolution of intelligence or self-annihilation. The galaxy is big, dark, and dangerous - to say nothing of the universe as a whole! Odds are, even if life was common on every planet, we'll be alone for our duration of existence in the universe.

Schrödinger's cat is a thought experiment, sometimes described as a paradox, devised by Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger in 1935. It illustrates what he saw as the problem of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics applied to everyday objects.

Schrödinger's cat: a cat, a flask of poison, and a radioactive source are placed in a sealed box. If an internal monitor detects radioactivity (i.e. a single atom decaying), the flask is shattered, releasing the poison that kills the cat. The Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics implies that after a while, the cat is simultaneously alive and dead. Yet, when one looks in the box, one sees the cat either alive or dead, not both alive and dead. This poses the question of when exactly quantum superposition ends and reality collapses into one possibility or the other.
